content: 1. If the heart rate is less than 100 beats per minute, take corrective steps to improve ventilation. 2. Continue ventilating at a rate of 40 breaths per minute. 3. Consider administering oxygen at a higher concentration. 4. Perform suctioning if necessary to clear the airway. 5. Provide routine care and closely monitor the patient’s breathing to ensure it remains adequate. 6. If the heart rate remains below 100 beats per minute, initiate chest compressions until the heart rate is at or above 100 beats per minute. 7. Administer oxygen at a higher concentration during resuscitation efforts. 8. If the heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute, consider additional ventilatory support or intravenous administration of adrenaline. The Pocket Book is designed for use by healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and other health workers, who are responsible for the care of young children in first-level referral hospitals. This second edition is based on evidence from several updated and published clinical guidelines by the World Health Organization (WHO). It is intended for both inpatient and outpatient care in small hospitals equipped with basic laboratory facilities and essential medicines. In some settings, these guidelines can also be applied in any facility where sick children are admitted for inpatient care. The Pocket Book is part of a series of documents and tools supporting the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI). The guidelines require hospitals to have the capacity to perform essential investigations, such as pulse oximetry, blood glucose measurement, blood smear examinations for malaria parasites, hemoglobin estimation, packed cell volume and full blood count, blood grouping and cross-matching, and basic microscopy of cerebrospinal fluid and urine. Where possible, facilities should also provide blood and urine cultures, ultrasound, and basic X-rays. Additionally, hospitals must have essential medicines for the treatment of seriously ill children. However, advanced treatment options, such as intensive care or mechanical ventilation, are not covered in these guidelines. The focus of these guidelines is on managing the major causes of childhood mortality in developing countries, including neonatal problems, pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, meningitis, septicemia, measles and related conditions, severe acute malnutrition, and pediatric HIV/AIDS. The guidelines also address some common surgical conditions that can be managed in small hospitals. Details of the evidence supporting the Pocket Book can be found on the WHO website, referencing the published guidelines listed in the bibliography. These guidelines are applicable in most regions globally and can be adapted to suit specific country circumstances. The online version will be updated regularly as new evidence becomes available.
